name: Quit smoking
lead: Quitting smoking is a lifestyle change that appearance communities discuss as a way to improve skin tone and texture, slow premature wrinkling and support the look of the teeth, breath, under-eye area and face generally. Dermatology references describe a pattern called smoker's face, with wrinkling, sagging and a greyish or sallow complexion, and tobacco smoke is described as accelerating extrinsic skin ageing.[5][6] The UK's NHS says that better oxygen flow to the skin after quitting can make it look brighter and that tar staining of the teeth stops.[12]

Most formal research on cessation concerns disease and mortality. A US national analysis of 113,752 women and 88,496 men found large survival benefits from quitting at various ages, and public health agencies report that counselling and approved medications raise quit rates.[1][3] Reviews also document oral effects of tobacco such as staining, gum disease, tooth loss and bad breath, which are part of how a smoker's face and mouth look.[7]

Looksmaxxing forums commonly list quitting among the foundational steps for skin, teeth and general health, and fitness communities such as T Nation treat it as a milestone alongside training changes.[8] Studies that directly measure facial appearance or periorbital darkness after quitting are few; the claim that stopping improves dark circles rests largely on community reports and on the documented circulation and skin effects of smoking.[6]

chain: Less oxidative stress and collagen breakdown, better oxygen and nutrient supply to skin
Healthier skin tone, fewer smoking-related wrinkles, cleaner teeth and gums
angle.text: People who quit report brighter skin colour and fresher-looking faces, and dermatology sources link smoking to wrinkling, a sallow complexion and stained teeth. Quitting removes that exposure, and the weeks-to-years timeline of improvement in circulation is documented for general health.

paras: In appearance discussion, quitting is cited for skin colour, texture and ageing, for dark circles and for the teeth and breath. A 1985 BMJ paper by D. Model described smoker's face as a cluster of features seen in about 46% of continuing smokers, 8% of former smokers who had smoked for a decade, and none of the non-smoking controls, as summarised in Wikipedia's article on the topic.[6] Forum users describe quitting as the change that made skin look less grey, in posts such as one T Nation user's account that after a week their skin 'has color'.[8]

The appearance-linked benefits that agencies describe are concrete: the NHS lists brighter-looking skin from better oxygen delivery, an end to tar staining of teeth, and returning taste and smell within days to weeks.[12] Wikipedia's smoker's face article lists the facial and oral features associated with smoking as wrinkles, sagging, a greyish tone, hair loss, gum disease, tooth loss, staining and bad breath.[6]

Smoking is a leading cause of preventable death, linked to heart disease, stroke, COPD and many cancers, and cessation lowers those risks. The CDC lists heart rate falling within minutes, blood nicotine reaching zero within 24 hours, heart attack risk dropping sharply within one to two years, and lung cancer risk halving after about ten to fifteen years.[11] Wikipedia reports a similar timeline and notes that British Doctors Study data found people who stopped before age 30 lived almost as long as lifelong non-smokers.[5]

sections.h: Effects of smoking on skin and mouth
paras: Descriptions of smoker's face attribute the changes to several mechanisms. Smoking raises matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes that break down collagen and elastin, lowers antioxidants such as vitamin C, adds reactive oxygen species, and narrows blood vessels so the skin receives less oxygen and nutrition.[6] Dermatology sources classify this as extrinsic ageing, caused by external factors rather than the passage of time.[6]

A review in Addiction describes tobacco's oral effects including periodontitis, caries, halitosis and oral cancer, and notes dental practitioners are placed to offer brief quit interventions.[7] Wikipedia's health-effects article says about half of periodontitis cases are attributed to current or former smoking, tooth loss is two to three times higher in smokers, and smoking stains teeth and causes bad breath.[2]
Smoking also reduces blood supply and is described as able to worsen conditions such as eczema; fingers of heavy smokers can show nicotine staining.[2]

sections.h: Origins and spread of the quitting movement
paras: The medical consensus that tobacco causes disease formed through the early to mid twentieth century: Wikipedia notes researchers linking tobacco with cancers in the 1930s, widely publicised US and UK studies in 1950, and acceptance by the medical community and the public in the mid-1960s.[2] Population cessation then became a public health goal, with national quitlines, awareness days such as the Great American Smokeout and World No Tobacco Day on 31 May, and smoke-free laws that are estimated to raise quit rates.[5]

The CDC reported that quitting among US adults rose between 2000 and 2015, and a later CDC report found about 70 percent of current smokers said they wanted to quit.[3][5] By 2018, 61.7% of US adults who had ever smoked had quit, up from 51.7% in 2009, according to Wikipedia's summary.[5]

Approaches include unassisted quitting, behavioural counselling, quitlines and apps, and medications such as nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline, bupropion and cytisine. A Wikipedia summary reports that unassisted attempts succeed long term in roughly 3 to 6 percent of cases, that people make an estimated 6 to 30 attempts before quitting for good, and that combining medication with behavioural support improves odds; a 2018 meta-analysis of 61 randomised trials reported about 20 percent abstinence at a year with treatment versus 12 percent with placebo.[5]

A Cochrane network meta-analysis of behavioural interventions examined how mode, intensity and delivery affect abstinence at six months.[9] CDC surveillance reports state that individual, group and telephone counselling and seven FDA-approved medications increase quit rates.[3] A Nature Reviews Disease Primers overview says most people who smoke relapse, and calls for wider reach of effective psychosocial and drug treatments.[13]

Electronic cigarettes are used by many smokers trying to stop. Wikipedia cites a 2022 study in which about 20 percent of smokers using them to quit succeeded but two thirds were dual users a year later, and a 2023 umbrella review of 400 publications found conclusive evidence linking e-cigarette use with poisoning, acute inhalation toxicity and lung injury.[5][14]

Nicotine acts on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and the brain's reward system, and withdrawal can involve cravings, irritability, poor sleep and low mood.[10][13] Wikipedia says cravings can persist for three to eight weeks and that a 2021 review associated quitting with reduced anxiety and depression.[5] A 2007 Science study found smokers with damage to the brain's insula often quit easily, which researchers took as evidence that region supports the urge to smoke.[15]

A national cohort reported weight gain after cessation, a concern some quitters cite when weighing appearance goals; Wikipedia summarises average gain at around 4 to 5 kg in the first year, mostly in the first three months.[4][5]

In forums quitting appears as a baseline health and skin step, often described with personal milestones rather than measurements. A T Nation member wrote a week after quitting that breathing was easier and that their skin had colour, and members of the same threads joke about smoking and training goals.[8] Community posts on eye bags and dark circles sometimes list smoking among contributing habits, though no study has tested this directly.[6]

No studies found on quitting smoking and under-eye appearance. Large studies of cessation address mortality, disease and quit rates, including the NEJM cohort of more than 200,000 US adults and the CDC analyses of quit attempts from 2000 to 2015.[1][3] Facial skin findings come from cross-sectional and descriptive work such as the BMJ smoker's face paper and dermatology reviews.[6]

timeline.event: US and UK researchers publish findings linking smoking with disease that attract wide attention.[2]
D. Model publishes 'Smoker's face: an underrated clinical sign?' in the BMJ on 21 December.[6]
A national US cohort quantifies weight gain after smoking cessation.[4]
Science reports that insula damage can disrupt cigarette addiction.[15]
NEJM analysis reports US hazards of smoking and benefits of quitting at different ages.[1]
CDC reports on quitting trends among US adults 2000-2015.[3]
A meta-analysis of 61 trials reports about 20 percent abstinence at a year with cessation drugs versus 12 percent with placebo.[5]
A Cochrane network meta-analysis compares behavioural interventions for quitting.[9]
An umbrella review assesses e-cigarette health outcomes across 400 publications.[14]

lore.intro: Quitting smoking appears in appearance threads as a baseline skin and health step, and in fitness forums as a lifestyle milestone; claims usually concern skin colour, dark circles, teeth and weight.[8]

claims.claim: Smoking worsens dark circles and quitting improves them
claims.believers: Proponents say smoking harms circulation and skin, so stopping lets the under-eye area recover; this is mostly stated as reasoning from general smoking effects rather than measured results.[8]
claims.experts: Reference sources document circulation and skin-condition effects of smoking; no published study has specifically tested periorbital darkness after quitting.[2][6]

claims.claim: Quitting brings back skin colour within weeks
claims.believers: A T Nation member wrote a week after quitting that breathing was easier and their skin had colour.[8]
claims.experts: Health sources describe circulation improving within about three months of quitting; facial skin recovery timelines are not well characterised.[5]

claims.claim: Smoker's face wrinkling is reduced after quitting
claims.believers: Users cite the smoker's-face concept to argue that stopping slows premature ageing.
claims.experts: The BMJ study found the features in about 46% of continuing smokers versus 8% of former smokers; the Wikipedia summary notes it does not state whether changes reverse.[6]

claims.claim: Weight gain after quitting offsets the benefit
claims.believers: Some forum members delay quitting over fear of gaining fat.
claims.experts: A national cohort documented weight gain after cessation, and health sources note cardiovascular benefits of quitting.[4][5]

claims.claim: Vaping or nicotine alternatives avoid the skin and teeth effects of smoking
claims.believers: Some users switch to vaping or nicotine products to keep nicotine while dropping tar and smoke, expecting cleaner teeth and skin.
claims.experts: A 2023 umbrella review found conclusive evidence linking e-cigarette use to poisoning, inhalation toxicity and lung injury; studies of e-cigarettes and facial appearance are not reported there.[14]

claims.claim: Quitting gives a fast 'glow' because of better oxygen supply
claims.believers: Users describe skin 'colour' returning within a week.[8] The NHS likewise says better oxygen flow can make skin look brighter.[12]
claims.experts: The CDC timeline reports carbon monoxide returning to non-smoker levels within days; facial skin recovery timelines are not well characterised in the literature.[11][6]

claims.claim: Quitting is hard and usually needs several attempts
claims.believers: Forum members describe repeated quit attempts and relapse during training and diet changes.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports an estimated 6 to 30 attempts before lasting abstinence and a long-term success rate of about 3 to 6 percent for unassisted attempts; medication plus support raises odds.[5]

card.summary: Quitting smoking is well supported for health; its effect on dark circles is untested.
card.note: Health benefits are documented; appearance benefit is not directly studied.

quick.overview:
Quitting smoking has well-documented health benefits. Appearance communities add that it may help skin and dark circles.

The cessation research cited here covers disease and mortality, not under-eye appearance.
quick.mechanism: Smoking reduces circulation and affects skin; stopping lets risk and some functions gradually improve.
quick.risks: Withdrawal can be distressing at first and some weight gain is reported after quitting. Clinicians and health agencies offer cessation support and approved medications.
